Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

# Liberal Democrats 2005 Manifesto Summary: "The Real Alternative"

## Core Principles and Political Position

The Liberal Democrats present themselves as Britain's progressive alternative, having "come of age" during the 2001-2005 parliament. The party distinguishes itself through principled opposition to Labour on Iraq, civil liberties, Council Tax, tuition fees, and ID cards—positioning themselves as "the real opposition" to an "increasingly discredited Government."

Three guiding principles underpin the manifesto: **Freedom** (individual self-governance free from unnecessary state interference), **Fairness** (ensuring essential requirements for genuine choice—education, pensions, healthcare, clean environment), and **Trust** (bringing government closer to citizens through democratic accountability and decentralised power).

## Fiscal Responsibility and Taxation

The party emphasises transparent, costed policies—a distinction from other parties. They propose redirecting approximately £5 billion annually from low-priority programmes, including abolishing the DTI, scrapping the Child Trust Fund, and rejecting ID cards.

Their flagship tax reform replaces Council Tax with Local Income Tax based on ability to pay, saving typical households £450 annually. A new 50% tax rate on income exceeding £100,000 (affecting 1% of taxpayers) funds three priorities: abolishing tuition/top-up fees (£1.2bn), free personal care for elderly/disabled (£1.7bn), and reducing local taxes (£2bn).

## Healthcare

The NHS requires liberation from Whitehall interference. Proposals include free personal care for the elderly, quicker diagnosis pathways, abolition of eye/dental check-up charges, and expanding prescription charge exemptions. The party commits to recruiting 8,000 doctors, 12,000 nurses, and 18,000 therapists while eliminating "absurd targets" that undermine professional judgement.

## Education

Investment priorities include abolishing all tuition fees, cutting infant class sizes to 20 pupils (using £1.5bn from scrapped Child Trust Fund), and guaranteeing specialist teachers for core subjects. A new diploma system would combine GCSE, A-level and vocational pathways.

## Crime and Civil Liberties

The manifesto strongly opposes ID cards as expensive and ineffective, redirecting funds to 10,000 additional police officers. It defends fundamental liberties against erosion—opposing house arrest powers, restrictions on jury trial, and detention without proper judicial process. The Prevention of Terrorism Act would be repealed, with terrorist suspects prosecuted through mainstream courts.

## Pensions and Welfare

A "Citizen's Pension" based on residency (not national insurance contributions) would guarantee £109.45 weekly for over-75s, addressing discrimination against women who interrupted careers for caring responsibilities. The manifesto proposes scrapping the failing Child Support Agency, reforming the New Deal, and extending Winter Fuel Payments to severely disabled people.

## Environment

Environmental policy constitutes "a strong green thread" throughout. Commitments include 20% renewable electricity by 2020, no replacement of nuclear power stations, carbon taxation reform, promoting public transport, and zero municipal waste goals. Climate change is identified as "the greatest man-made threat to the planet."

## Europe and International Affairs

The party explicitly opposed the Iraq War as illegal and based on flawed intelligence, whilst accepting moral obligations toward Iraqi stability. They support EU membership and constitutional reform, advocate UN strengthening, and commit to reaching 0.7% GNI in development aid by 2011.

## Democratic Reform

Proposals include curbing Prime Ministerial power, introducing a War Powers Act, implementing proportional representation (STV) for elections, and creating a predominantly elected second chamber. Local government would receive substantially enhanced autonomy from Whitehall control.

The manifesto concludes with ten contrasts against opponents: patients over targets, scrapping fees, police over ID cards, free care, environmental action, smaller classes, pension increases, tax transparency, fair local taxation, and rejecting the Iraq War approach.

# Green Party Manifesto 2005: Summary

## A Vision for Sustainable Society

The Green Party presents a comprehensive programme built on social, economic and environmental justice, placing people and planetary resources at the heart of policy. The manifesto challenges the Westminster status quo, which has created widening inequality, eroded public services, and ignored environmental destruction.

## Economic Transformation

The Greens propose radical economic reform, arguing that current stability rests on short-term wealth creation, resource overuse, and gross inequality. Their approach treats natural resources as finite capital rather than disposable income, implementing progressive taxation with higher rates for top earners (50% above £50,000, 60% above £100,000). VAT would be replaced with eco-taxes reflecting environmental costs. The party champions economic localisation over globalisation, supporting community banks, credit unions, and local currencies whilst opposing euro membership. A Citizen's Income and Citizen's Pension would provide universal security, reducing means-testing and empowering individuals.

## Climate Change and Energy

Climate change represents the gravest environmental and economic threat. The Greens adopt the Contraction and Convergence framework, targeting 20% carbon reduction by 2010 and 85% by 2030. This includes carbon taxation, 40% renewable energy by 2020, and closure of nuclear power stations. A Warmer Homes Act would reduce domestic energy demand by 30%.

## Public Services

The manifesto demands restoration of the NHS to founding principles—comprehensive, universal care based on need—rejecting privatisation, foundation hospitals, and Public-Private Partnerships. Health funding would rise to EU average levels. Education policy includes scrapping tuition fees, restoring maintenance grants, abolishing SATs, and introducing individualised learning.

## Transport Revolution

Transport policy prioritises sustainable modes: walking, cycling, and public transport over private cars and aviation. Rail and tube networks would return to public ownership. Motoring would reflect true environmental costs through congestion charging and fuel duties, while aviation fuel taxation would end the industry's effective £9 billion annual subsidy.

## Environmental Protection

A Zero Waste Strategy would outlaw incineration and target 60% recycling by 2010. The precautionary principle would govern new technologies including genetic modification. Animal rights would be extended, with bans on blood sports, battery cages, and live exports.

## Food and Farming

The Organics Target Bill would achieve 30% organic production by 2012. The Common Agricultural Policy, promoting unsustainable industrialised farming, would be replaced with support for local food markets and smaller farms. Genetically modified food would be banned.

## Crime and Communities

Crime reduction focuses on prevention through strong communities, improved urban design, youth facilities, and addressing social causes. Community policing would increase, with restorative justice central to the system. Strict gun control legislation would be implemented, whilst national ID cards are opposed.

## Democratic Renewal

Constitutional reform would devolve power to local communities, introduce proportional representation, and create an elected House of Lords. The proposed EU constitution fails democratic and sustainability tests; the Greens campaign for rejection whilst remaining committed to European engagement.

## International Justice

A truly ethical foreign policy would replace militarism with peaceful diplomacy. UK nuclear weapons would be decommissioned, arms sales ended, and overseas aid increased to 1% of GNI. Debt cancellation for the 52 poorest countries would promote stability. The World Trade Organisation would be reformed through a General Agreement on Sustainable Trade, favouring local economies over corporate globalisation. Asylum seekers would receive proper support and rights under international conventions.

The manifesto represents a political programme for the next hundred years, not merely the next hundred days—offering real choice for real change.
